title: Chapter 15
paragraphs: "That was the history of my beloved cottagers. It made a deep impression on me. From its picture of human society, I learned to admire their virtues and condemn humanity's vices.

"At that time I still saw crime as a distant evil. Kindness and generosity were always before me, inspiring a desire to play my own part in the busy world where so many admirable qualities were displayed. But in describing the development of my mind, I must mention something that happened in early August of that same year.

"One night, during my usual trip to the woods to gather my own food and bring home firewood for my protectors, I found a leather bag on the ground containing some clothes and several books. I eagerly grabbed this prize and took it to my hovel. Fortunately, the books were written in the language I'd been learning at the cottage. They were _Paradise Lost_, a volume of _Plutarch's Lives_, and _The Sorrows of Werter_. Possessing these treasures gave me immense delight. I studied them constantly while my friends were busy with their daily work.

"I can barely describe the effect these books had on me. They produced a flood of new images and emotions that sometimes lifted me to ecstasy but more often plunged me into the deepest misery. In _The Sorrows of Werter_, beyond the gripping simplicity of the story, so many opinions were explored and so much light thrown on subjects that had been dark to me that I found in it an endless source of wonder and reflection. Its descriptions of gentle domestic life, together with lofty feelings directed at something beyond the self, matched my experience of my protectors and the longings alive in my own heart. But I thought Werter himself a more godlike being than I'd ever seen or imagined. His character was unpretentious yet deeply moving. His reflections on death and suicide filled me with awe. I didn't presume to judge the merits of his case, but I leaned toward his views, and I wept at his death without precisely understanding it.

"As I read, I constantly applied what I found to my own feelings and situation. I found myself both similar to and strangely different from the people I read about and the people whose conversation I listened to. I could sympathize with them and partly understand them, but my mind was unformed. I depended on no one and was related to no one. 'The path of my departure was free,' and there was no one who would mourn my destruction. My body was hideous and my size enormous. What did this mean? Who was I? What was I? Where did I come from? What was my purpose? These questions kept returning, but I couldn't answer them.

"The volume of _Plutarch's Lives_ that I had contained the histories of the first founders of the ancient republics. This book had a very different effect on me from _The Sorrows of Werter_. From Werter I learned despondency and gloom. But Plutarch taught me to think nobly. He lifted me above my own wretched existence to admire and love the heroes of ancient times. Much of what I read was beyond my understanding and experience. I had only a vague idea of kingdoms, vast countries, mighty rivers, and boundless seas. I knew nothing about towns or large gatherings of people. The cottage was the only place I'd ever studied human nature. But Plutarch opened new and mightier scenes. I read of men in public life, governing or slaughtering their own species. I felt the greatest desire for virtue rise within me, and the deepest horror at vice — as far as I understood those terms, which for me were still tied simply to pleasure and pain. This led me to admire peaceful lawmakers like Numa, Solon, and Lycurgus over conquerors like Romulus and Theseus. My protectors' peaceful lives reinforced these feelings. Perhaps if my first encounter with humanity had been through a young soldier burning for glory and blood, I would have felt very differently.

"But _Paradise Lost_ stirred far deeper emotions. I read it — as I read the others — as true history. It filled me with every feeling of wonder and awe that the picture of an all-powerful God warring with his creatures could produce. I constantly compared the various situations to my own. Like Adam, I seemed connected to no other being in existence. But his condition was utterly different from mine in every other way. He had been created perfect by God — happy, fortunate, specially protected. He was allowed to speak with and learn from beings higher than himself. But I was wretched, helpless, and alone. Many times I saw Satan as a better image of my condition. Like him, when I saw the happiness of my protectors, bitter envy rose within me.

"Another discovery deepened these feelings. Soon after arriving at the hovel, I found some papers in the pocket of the clothes I'd taken from your laboratory. At first I'd ignored them. Now that I could read, I studied them carefully. They were your journal of the four months before my creation. You described every step of your work in detail, mixed with accounts of your daily life. You certainly remember these papers. Here they are. Everything about my cursed origin is in them — the complete, disgusting story of how I was made. The most minute description of my hideous body is given, in language that painted your own horror and made mine permanent. I felt sick as I read. 'Hateful day when I received life!' I cried in anguish. 'Cursed creator! Why did you make a monster so hideous that even _you_ turned away in disgust? God, in his mercy, made man beautiful, in his own image. But my form is a filthy copy of yours, made even more horrible by the very resemblance. Satan at least had companions — fellow demons to admire and encourage him. But I am utterly alone and despised.'

"These were my thoughts in hours of despair and isolation. But when I thought about my cottagers' virtues, their kind and generous natures, I convinced myself that when they learned of my admiration, they would pity me and overlook my physical ugliness. Could they really turn away someone, however monstrous, who asked for their compassion and friendship? I resolved not to give up hope but to prepare myself in every way for the encounter that would decide my fate. I postponed it for some months longer — the stakes were too high and the fear of failure too great. Besides, my understanding improved every day, and I didn't want to attempt it until a few more months had sharpened my mind.

"Meanwhile, changes took place in the cottage. Safie's presence had spread happiness, and I also found that the household now had more plenty than before. Felix and Agatha spent more time in conversation and entertainment, helped by servants. They didn't seem rich, but they were content and at peace. Their feelings were calm, while mine grew more turbulent every day. Growing knowledge only showed me more clearly what a wretched outcast I was. I held onto hope, but it vanished whenever I saw my reflection in water or my shadow in moonlight — as fleeting and unreal as those images themselves.

"I tried to crush these fears and steel myself for the trial I'd resolved to face in a few months. Sometimes I let my thoughts wander unchecked into dreams of paradise, imagining kind, lovely beings who understood my feelings and eased my darkness. Their angelic faces smiled with comfort. But it was all fantasy. No Eve soothed my sorrows or shared my thoughts. I was alone. I remembered Adam's plea to his Creator. But where was mine? He had abandoned me. In the bitterness of my heart, I cursed him.

"Autumn passed. I watched with surprise and sadness as the leaves decayed and fell and nature put on the barren, bleak appearance it had worn when I first saw the woods and the lovely moon. Yet I didn't mind the cold weather. My body was better suited to endure cold than heat. But my greatest pleasures had been flowers, birds, and all the bright display of summer. When these vanished, I turned with more attention to the cottagers. Their happiness wasn't diminished by summer's absence. They loved each other, and their joys depended on one another, undisturbed by what happened around them. The more I saw of them, the more I longed to claim their protection and kindness. My heart yearned to be known and loved by these kind people. To see their kind faces turned toward me with affection was the highest dream I could imagine. I didn't dare think they would look at me with contempt and horror. The poor who came to their door were never turned away. I asked, it's true, for more than a little food or rest. I needed kindness and understanding. But I didn't believe myself entirely unworthy of it.

"Winter came, and a full year had passed since I first woke into life. My attention was now focused entirely on my plan to introduce myself to the cottagers. I considered many approaches. The one I settled on was to enter the cottage when the blind old man was alone. I was smart enough to realize that my unnatural ugliness was the main source of horror for those who had seen me. My voice, though harsh, had nothing terrible about it. So I reasoned that if, in his children's absence, I could win the goodwill and help of old De Lacey, through him I might be tolerated by my younger protectors.

"One day, when the sun shone on the red leaves scattered on the ground and spread a cheerfulness that contradicted the cold, Safie, Agatha, and Felix left for a long walk in the country. The old man, at his own request, was left alone. When they'd gone, he took up his guitar and played several mournful but sweet melodies — sweeter and sadder than I'd ever heard from him. At first his face was lit with pleasure, but as he played on, thoughtfulness and sadness took over. Finally, setting aside the instrument, he sat absorbed in reflection.

"My heart beat fast. This was the hour that would determine my hopes or confirm my fears. The servants had gone to a nearby fair. Everything was silent in and around the cottage. It was the perfect opportunity. Yet when I moved to carry out my plan, my legs buckled and I collapsed to the ground. I rose again, summoned every ounce of courage I possessed, and removed the planks I'd placed over my hovel entrance to hide my retreat. Fresh air revived me. With renewed determination, I approached the cottage door.
"I knocked. 'Who is there?' said the old man. 'Come in.'
"I entered. 'Forgive the intrusion,' I said. 'I'm a traveler who needs a little rest. You'd greatly oblige me if you'd let me warm myself by your fire for a few minutes.'
"'Come in,' said De Lacey. 'I'll try to help however I can. But unfortunately my children are away from home, and since I'm blind, I'm afraid I can't easily find you food.'
"'Please don't trouble yourself, kind sir. I have food. I need only warmth and rest.'
"I sat down. A silence followed. I knew every minute was precious, yet I couldn't decide how to begin. Then the old man spoke.
"'From your language, stranger, I take it you're my countryman. Are you French?'
"'No, but I was educated by a French family and understand only that language. I'm now on my way to seek the protection of some friends whom I love dearly and in whose kindness I have some hope.'
"'Are they Germans?'

"'No, they're French. But let me change the subject. I'm an unfortunate and abandoned creature. I look around and have no relative or friend on earth. These kind people I'm going to have never seen me and know little of me. I'm full of fear, because if they reject me, I'll be an outcast forever.'

"'Don't despair. Being friendless is certainly a misfortune. But the hearts of men, when not clouded by self-interest, are full of brotherly love and charity. Trust in your hopes. If your friends are good and kind, don't give up.'

"'They are kind — they're the most excellent people in the world. But unfortunately they're prejudiced against me. I have good intentions. My life has been harmless and even somewhat beneficial. But a fatal prejudice blinds them. Where they should see a feeling, kind friend, they see only a detestable monster.'
"'That is indeed unfortunate. But if you're truly blameless, can't you set them right?'

"'I'm about to try exactly that. And it's this attempt that fills me with such overwhelming dread. I love these friends dearly. For many months, unknown to them, I've done them daily kindnesses. But they believe I mean them harm. That's the misunderstanding I'm trying to overcome.'
"'Where do these friends live?'
"'Near this very spot.'

"The old man paused, then continued: 'If you confide in me fully, perhaps I can help set things right. I'm blind and can't judge your face, but there's something in your words that convinces me you're sincere. I'm poor and an exile, but it would give me true pleasure to help a fellow human being.'
"'Excellent man! I thank you and accept your generous offer. You lift me from the dust with this kindness. I trust that with your help, I won't be driven from the company of your fellow creatures.'

"'Heaven forbid! Even if you were guilty of a crime — for that can only drive you to desperation, not inspire virtue. I too am unfortunate. My family and I have been condemned, though innocent. So judge whether I can't feel for your troubles.'

"'How can I thank you, my best and only friend? Yours is the first voice of kindness ever directed at me. I'll be grateful forever. Your goodness assures me I'll succeed with the friends I'm about to meet.'
"'May I know their names and where they live?'

"I paused. This was the moment of truth — the moment that would grant or destroy my happiness forever. I fought for the strength to answer, but the effort broke me. I collapsed into the chair and sobbed aloud. Just then I heard the footsteps of my younger protectors. There wasn't a moment to lose. Seizing the old man's hand, I cried, 'Now is the time! Save and protect me! You and your family are the friends I seek. Don't abandon me in this hour of need!'
"'Great God!' exclaimed the old man. 'Who are you?'

"At that instant the cottage door opened, and Felix, Safie, and Agatha entered. Who can describe their horror and shock at seeing me? Agatha fainted. Safie, unable to help her friend, rushed out of the cottage. Felix lunged forward and, with superhuman force, tore me from his father's knees where I clung. In a fury, he threw me to the ground and beat me violently with a stick. I could have torn him limb from limb, as the lion tears apart the antelope. But my heart sank with bitter anguish, and I held back. When I saw him about to strike again, overcome by pain and grief, I fled the cottage. In the confusion, I escaped unnoticed to my hovel."
